summary:
Visitors in Zamfara stand under two overlapping layers of criminal law. At the national level Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct through the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), which the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sex between men under secular law. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documents that the Act reaches well beyond marriage: it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The statute binds all persons present in the country, tourists included.

Layered on top is Sharia criminal law. The same Home Office note records that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Zamfara is where this second layer began. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report on the extension of Sharia to criminal law records that Zamfara's governor was first to move, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000; by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and these remain the only states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases. A visitor in Zamfara is therefore inside the original and fully operative instance of the regime, not a peripheral one.

Zamfara's own account of the adoption, given by its then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000, sets out the enabling legislation: the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999, enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution, which established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and enabled the codification of a Sharia Penal Code. The Grand Kadi took over court administration on 29 June 2000. A Zamfara committee appointed in June 1999 had been mandated to study implementing Sharia including the full scope of Islamic criminal law; by the end of 2000 eleven other northern states had adopted its application.

The codification of offences and punishments produced a penal-code architecture that the Sharia courts of all twelve states now apply, a framework Zamfara pioneered across the northern bloc. Trans identity itself is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed: Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Violence risk is documented and unresolved. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation, but The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion.
tangentialFactors:
Zamfara's pioneering role cuts both ways. The model it drafted in 1999 was copied by eleven further northern states within a year and by twelve by 2002, so the penal-code architecture a visitor faces in Zamfara is the same architecture operative across a large part of the country, while the states involved remain the only ones where Sharia courts can try criminal cases at all.

Enforcement climate diverges from statutory text. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing hostility independent of its words, and the documented cases against perceived gay people — a Lagos street stop producing a gun-butt injury and a partial bribe payment in March 2025 — arise under the secular statute, far from any Sharia court.

Indictment exposure also differs by charge. Bobrisky's six-month sentence was imposed for financial offences, not for gender expression, yet an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender; placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion throughout.

Court administration passed to the Grand Kadi on 29 June 2000.

Implementation in Zamfara began with a governor-appointed committee in June 1999 mandated to study carrying out Sharia including the full scope of Islamic criminal law, followed by policy moves against prostitution and gambling and the entry into force of the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 January 2000.

Residents live under both statutory and Sharia criminal regimes simultaneously: the SSMPA's 10-to-14-year penalties apply nationally, while the codified Sharia Penal Code supplies the offences and punishments heard by the twelve states' courts.

Trans residents have no statutory recognition and no legal protections as LGBTQ+ people; detention placement for a trans detainee between male and female sections is not governed by a written rule in the documented cases, and the Nigerian Correctional Service Act was found to have been breached in the placement of a first-time offender in a maximum-security facility in October 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing have been enacted is unresolved: Reuters reports the proposals and the fear they generated, but the sources assembled here do not settle their legislative status.

Whether a sentence of death has actually been imposed for same-sex conduct in Zamfara is not established here. The sources establish that the death penalty is available under state Zina provisions and that the twelve states' courts are capital-punishment-capable, not that a capital sentence for this conduct has been handed down.

Whether Zamfara's Sharia criminal jurisdiction extends to non-Muslim residents or visitors, and the practical extent of its application to women under Zina provisions, are not addressed by the inventory sources.

The disposition of the August 2024 killing of the Abuja TikToker remains open: no suspects had been charged six months on, and later outcomes are not sourced here.
